article.title: How to Spot a Fake Bottle of Premium Spirits
article.body:
How to Spot a Fake Bottle of Premium Spirits

Check the seal, the label, the fill level and the batch code, and be wary of any price far below other licensed retailers. Genuine bottles have tight, unbroken closures, crisp printing and matching codes on bottle and box. Drinks House 247 recommends buying premium spirits only from licensed UK retailers with traceable stock.

Counterfeit spirits fall into two very different groups. At the cheap end, Trading Standards teams in the UK regularly warn about fake vodka and other spirits made with industrial alcohol, which can be genuinely dangerous. At the luxury end, the risk is refilled bottles and imitation labels on rare whisky, cognac and tequila, which cost buyers a great deal of money. The checks for both are similar, and most take a few seconds.

The quick checklist

Check What a genuine bottle looks like Warning signs
PriceIn line with other licensed retailersA price far below everyone else, especially on a rare bottle
Seal and closureTight capsule or intact tamper ring; cap turns only when brokenLoose capsule, glue marks, a cap that turns freely, a broken or missing ring
LabelStraight, crisp printing, consistent fonts, correct spellingBlurred print, spelling mistakes, peeling edges, label on crooked
Fill levelThe same level as other bottles of the same productNoticeably high or low fill, or different levels across bottles in a case
Batch or laser codePresent, cleanly printed on the glass or label, and matching the boxMissing, scratched off, or different from the code on the box
The liquidClear spirits are perfectly clear; aged spirits are an even colourFloating particles, cloudiness, or a colour unlike the usual bottle
SmellSmells like the spirit shouldA sharp chemical or nail-varnish smell
The sellerA licensed retailer with a real address and clear contact detailsAnonymous marketplace listings, cash-only sales, no receipt

Why price is the first warning sign

Premium spirits are priced within a fairly narrow band across legitimate UK retailers, because duty and the brand's own pricing leave little room for dramatic discounts. When a rare whisky or luxury tequila is offered for a fraction of what reputable shops charge, the most likely explanation is that something is wrong with it. A bargain on a bottle that is famously hard to find is the single biggest red flag.

The refilled-bottle problem

At the luxury end, a genuine bottle is no proof of genuine contents. Empty bottles of expensive spirits, especially distinctive decanters and ceramic bottles, are resold online, and some are refilled with something cheaper. That is why the closure matters more than the glass:

  • Look for any sign the capsule or seal has been removed and reapplied.
  • Check that a screw cap's tamper ring is intact and still attached.
  • Compare the stopper or cork against photographs from the brand itself.
  • Some prestige brands now add tamper-evident closures or unique codes that can be checked with the brand. Use them if they are there.

Rare and old bottles

For collectable whisky, cognac and other spirits bottled decades ago, forgeries can be sophisticated, with convincing labels and period-correct bottles. Serious buyers rely on provenance: a documented history of where the bottle has been, and receipts from reputable auction houses or retailers. Specialist laboratories can analyse a sample to test whether the spirit's age matches its label. If a rare bottle comes with no history at all, treat that as a warning.

Cheap counterfeit spirits can be dangerous

Illicit spirits made outside a licensed distillery can contain methanol or other industrial alcohols, which can cause serious harm. The Food Standards Agency and Trading Standards advise watching for:

  • A price that seems too good to be true.
  • Spelling mistakes, poor printing or a label that does not look right.
  • A smell of nail varnish or chemicals.
  • Bottles sold outside licensed premises, such as from car boots or door to door.

If you have drunk something you suspect is counterfeit and feel unwell, particularly with blurred vision, vomiting or severe headache, seek medical help straight away.

What should you do if you suspect a fake?

  1. Do not drink it.
  2. Keep the bottle, packaging and receipt, and note where and when you bought it.
  3. Contact the seller if they are a legitimate business. A reputable retailer will want to know.
  4. Report it. In England and Wales, the Citizens Advice consumer helpline passes reports to Trading Standards. In Scotland, contact Advice Direct Scotland, and in Northern Ireland, Consumerline.
  5. Tell the brand. Most major spirits producers have a team that investigates counterfeits of their products.

The best defence

Checking seals and labels helps, but the most reliable protection is where you buy. A licensed UK retailer has to hold a premises licence, and legitimate retailers buy through traceable supply chains. They have a reputation and a licence to lose, and they are accountable if something goes wrong. That is worth more than any checklist, particularly for a special or expensive bottle.

Frequently asked questions

How can you tell if a bottle of spirits is fake?

Check that the seal is tight and unbroken, the label is crisply printed and correctly spelled, the fill level matches other bottles, and the batch code matches the box. A price far below other licensed retailers is the biggest warning sign.

Can a genuine bottle contain fake alcohol?

Yes. Empty bottles of expensive spirits are sometimes resold and refilled with cheaper spirit. That is why an intact seal, capsule and tamper ring matter more than the bottle itself.

Is fake alcohol dangerous?

It can be. Illicit spirits may contain methanol or other industrial alcohols. If you feel unwell after drinking suspect alcohol, especially with blurred vision or vomiting, seek medical help straight away.

Where should you report counterfeit alcohol in the UK?

In England and Wales, contact the Citizens Advice consumer helpline, which passes reports to Trading Standards. In Scotland, contact Advice Direct Scotland, and in Northern Ireland, Consumerline.
